light_fc_min — removed on audit: Band-level number presented as a species value, taken from a source that contradicts itself about this exact species. I fetched the Clemson factsheet: the table row is only "Hedera helix and cultivars | English Ivy" sitting under a header that reads "Medium light (100 to 150 ft-c)" — a range, not a minimum, and 150 is its TOP. The band definition on the same page is "Medium (minimum 100 to 150 ft-c, 200 to 500 preferred)" — again a range, so there is no single stated minimum to take; picking 150 over 100 is an undisclosed editorial choice that doubles the requirement. Worse, the SAME factsheet's prose names this species a high-light plant ("High light plants (weeping fig, English ivy, schefflera)..."), whose band is "minimum 150 to 1000 ft-c, 500 to 1000 preferred". The record's own citation block admits this conflict and then takes the Medium number anyway rather than treating the field as unresolved. Finally, the only species-specific footcandle figure anywhere in the evidence set points the other way: UF/IFAS EP243 says ivy holds its appearance at 100 fc. Nothing on any admissible page states 150 fc as this species' minimum.

light_fc_good — removed on audit: 200 is a class-level figure, not a species figure. It comes solely from the definition sentence "Medium (minimum 100 to 150 ft-c, 200 to 500 preferred)". The table where Hedera helix actually appears carries only "100 to 150 ft-c" in its header — the preferred number is nowhere near the species row, so this fails the test that a table listing establishes a number only when the band's numbers are in the quote with it. It is also contradicted twice over: the same factsheet's prose classes English ivy as high light (preferred 500 to 1000), and UF/IFAS's species-specific statement says 100 fc suffices to maintain appearance. Picking the bottom of one band's preferred range while the same document assigns the species to a different band is arbitrary.

night_f_min — removed on audit: No night temperature is printed on the Clemson page — I confirmed the only sentence is "Ivies do well at cool to moderate room temperatures of 50 to 70 °F during the day and about 5 to 10 °F lower at night." 40 is manufactured by compounding two worst cases (lowest day figure minus largest drop), and the word "about" rules out treating the drop as an exact bound. The record discloses the arithmetic, which is honest, but disclosure does not make 40 °F a sourced value. This is the safety-relevant direction of the error: the only species-specific night statement in the entire evidence set is UF/IFAS EP243's "Plant quality and growth rates begin to decline when day temperatures routinely exceed 95°F or night temperatures drop below 65°F," so a stated-acceptable night floor of 40 °F sits 25 °F below the one documented night threshold and is endorsed by no admissible source. The citation label also reads "night_f", which is not a field name in this schema.

night_f_max — removed on audit: Same defect as night_f_min: derived, not stated. No night figure appears on the Clemson page; 65 is 70 minus the smaller end of an approximate ("about 5 to 10 °F") drop. The arithmetic is internally valid but the value is a construction, and the source's hedge makes precise endpoints unwarranted. Note also that the record's entire night band (40-65) lies at or below UF/IFAS's stated decline point of 65 °F, so the derived range coincidentally tops out exactly where the only species-specific evidence says quality already starts falling off — a coincidence the record never reconciles.

day_f_max — removed on audit: The value 70 matches the quote, but its citation is broken: the claim label reads "day_f 50-75". 75 appears nowhere on the Clemson page (I checked the live text — it says 50 to 70 °F) and contradicts the record's own stored value of 70. An evidence label carrying a number the source does not contain is not a traceable citation, and a downstream reader reconciling label against value gets a 5 °F discrepancy with no way to tell which is authoritative. The label also leads with "day_f", which is not the exact field name for either day_f_min or day_f_max.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The quote is verbatim-accurate (I confirmed the full Poison Symptoms string on the live NC State page), but the record's prose rendering silently deletes the severe half of it. NC State reads "Ingestion of leaves can result in delirium, stupor, convulsions, hallucinations, fever and rash, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypersalivation, and diarrhea." The record reports only "vomiting, abdominal pain, hypersalivation and diarrhea" — dropping delirium, stupor, convulsions, hallucinations and fever. It likewise softens "severe skin irritation with redness, itching, and blisters" to "contact dermatitis". In the one field whose purpose is to tell an owner how serious an ingestion is, the summary understates the source it cites. Separately, NC State's Poison Symptoms text is human-oriented (the page tags "Poisonous to Humans" and says "English ivy contains allergens that may affect humans"); the pet claim rests only on the Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags, which carry no symptoms at all. Presenting the human symptom list as pet-toxicity detail without flagging that distinction is a species-of-victim conflation.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: Clemson's monthly interval is explicitly conditional — "Fertilize ivies monthly while they are actively growing" followed by "Do not use fertilizer when plants stop growing either in the heat of summer, or when temperatures are cool." The record stores 30 as an unconditional interval and leaves fertilize_active_months null, so the source's prohibition survives nowhere in the structured fields; it exists only inside a citation quote and an unknowns note. Paired with fertilize_strength "full", the record as stored reads as year-round full-label-rate feeding, which is the specific practice the cited sentence forbids. The number is faithful to the word "monthly"; the encoding drops the condition that makes it safe.

name_note — removed on audit: The note asserts that "UF/IFAS, UGA, Clemson, Penn State — still publish under Saintpaulia ionantha," and uses that bridge to justify treating all four as species-level evidence for this plant. Two of the four are misdescribed. Clemson HGIC 1550 prints its botanical name as "Saintpaulia species" — genus level, no epithet at all. Penn State's African Violet Care page carries no binomial whatsoever, only the common name. Only UF/IFAS (MG028 and EP360) and UGA C660 actually name Saintpaulia ionantha, as the record claims. This is not cosmetic: Clemson is one of only two citations holding up day_f_max 85, so the record's own justification for admitting that source is false.

day_f_max — removed on audit: 85 is the single highest day ceiling anywhere in the corpus, and both citations are weaker than presented. Clemson's sentence is verbatim, but that factsheet is genus-level ("Saintpaulia species"), not a species record. UF/IFAS EP360's "When the day temperature exceeds 85°F, plant growth and flowering are stunted" is verbatim but comes from a commercial greenhouse production guideline, and the same page's actual optimum is "An average day temperature of 77°F provides the highest rate of vegetative growth." Meanwhile three admissible sources that treat this species as a houseplant all cap the range at 80 °F: NC State's own S. ionanthus page ("Maintaining a temperature between 60 and 80 degrees is optimum"), UF/IFAS MG028 ("will grow satisfactorily at 60 to 80°F"), and Penn State ("thrive in the same range that we enjoy, between 60°F and 80°F"). The record cites none of the three for this field and does not disclose the conflict.

day_f_min — removed on audit: Sole support is UGA's "The most attractive violets are grown at a nighttime temperature of 65 °F to 70 °F and a daytime temperature of 70 °F to 90 °F" — verbatim, but an aesthetic-optimum statement, not a minimum. The record keeps that sentence's 70 °F floor while silently discarding its 90 °F ceiling (day_f_max is set to 85 from unrelated sources), so half of one sentence was adopted and half rejected with no stated rationale. Three admissible species-level sources contradict a 70 °F daytime floor outright: NC State ("between 60 and 80 degrees is optimum"), UF/IFAS MG028 ("will grow satisfactorily at 60 to 80°F"), and Penn State ("between 60°F and 80°F"). A 70 °F floor would flag a 65 °F room as too cold when three sources say it is fine.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: 28 is a point estimate manufactured from a range. The UGA quote is verbatim but says "Most violet hobbyists prefer to use liquid or water-soluble fertilizers such as 20-20-20 every four to six weeks" — reported hobbyist practice, not an extension recommendation, and nothing in it privileges the 4-week end over the 6-week end. The record chose the shortest interval, i.e. the most fertilizer, for a plant the immediately adjacent sentence of that same source calls "very sensitive to a build-up of soluble salt which can damage plant roots." It also conflicts irreconcilably with admissible UF/IFAS MG028, which prescribes a categorically different regime ("Mix the fertilizer in water at one-fourth the recommended rate and apply it each time you water"); the record acknowledges the conflict and resolves it by fiat with no reason given.

fertilize_strength — removed on audit: "half" sits literally inside UGA's "one-third to one-half the recommended amount of fertilizer," but it is the top of that range, and the only other admissible source on dosing, UF/IFAS MG028, specifies "one-fourth the recommended rate." Across the corpus the sourced range is one-fourth to one-half and the record selected the maximum, with no rationale offered, for a plant UGA warns is "very sensitive to a build-up of soluble salt which can damage plant roots." Combined with fertilize_interval_days 28 — also the maximum-feeding end of its range — both fertilizer fields land on the highest-dose corner of the evidence, which is the harm-increasing direction for this species.

humidity_pct_min — removed on audit: The only humidity percentage anywhere in the corpus comes from UF/IFAS EP360, whose "Saintpaulia grows well at 50% to 70% relative humidity" I confirmed verbatim — but EP360 is "Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production," a greenhouse crop specification. Its surrounding text is explicitly facility guidance ("Maintain high humidity with mist or fogging"; "Humidity may be raised by wetting walkways and underneath benches with a hose"). Every admissible source that addresses African violets as a houseplant — MG028, NC State, Penn State — treats humidity only qualitatively and gives no number at all. The record converts a greenhouse production target into a home-care numeric floor without flagging the context shift, and NC State's own species page is self-contradictory on the point, tagging the plant "#dry air tolerant" while its body text says "It is intolerant of dry air."

humidity_pct_max — removed on audit: Same defect as humidity_pct_min: the 70% figure exists only in UF/IFAS EP360's commercial greenhouse production guideline, in a passage about mist and fog systems, and is presented in the record as a home-care requirement for the species. No admissible houseplant-oriented source in the corpus states any relative-humidity percentage, so the precision here is imported from a production context rather than established for indoor culture.

records.name_note: NC State and the RHS both file this species as Heptapleurum arboricola (the epithet ends -a, not -um, as given), with Schefflera arboricola listed as the former name/synonym. Missouri Botanical Garden and Clemson's schefflera factsheet still publish under Schefflera arboricola, and Clemson's indoor light table uses the older synonym Brassaia arboricola for "Dwarf Schefflera" — all four pages are describing the same plant.
records.cool_rest_note: No cool winter rest is described for this species: Missouri Botanical Garden keeps indoor temperatures above 60 °F through winter and only reduces watering somewhat from fall to late winter (the RHS likewise says water sparingly in winter).
records.toxicity_detail: All parts are seriously toxic to dogs and cats. Toxic principle is calcium oxalate crystals; poison parts are the leaves and sap/juice. Chewed leaves cause intense mouth and throat irritation, excessive drooling, difficulty swallowing and vomiting. NC State rates overall poison severity as Low, and notes the sap can irritate people with sensitive skin (causes contact dermatitis).

light_fc_min — removed on audit: Clemson never assigns a 150 ft-c floor to this species. The band definition reads "Medium (minimum 100 to 150 ft-c, 200 to 500 preferred)" and the table caption that actually contains this plant reads "Medium light (100 to 150 ft-c)" — the stated minimum is a range beginning at 100, and the researcher silently took the top of it as the species floor. Worse, the row for this plant carries the asterisk whose footnote the record itself quotes: "*May also be conditioned to grow in low light" — and Clemson's Low band is "minimum 100 ft-c". So the one species-specific qualifier on the page pushes the floor DOWN toward 100, and the record moved it UP to 150. Verified verbatim at hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/indoor-plants-cleaning-fertilizing-containers-light-requirements/. (light_fc_good 200 survives: it is the literal start of the Medium band's "200 to 500 preferred".)

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: This is an unresolved union of two sources that disagree, and it spans the entire possible range — "full sun" and "deep shade" simultaneously. "full sun" is not endorsed by either source: MOBOT's own Culture text (verified verbatim) says "Winter hardy to USDA Zones 10-12 where it is best grown in bright part shade locations. Outdoors, it tolerates full sun, but generally appreciates protection from direct sun during the heat of the day"; NC State says only "While it can tolerate some full sun outdoors..." and its structured Cultural Conditions Light list — the field the record is actually mirroring — stops at Dappled Sunlight / Deep shade / Partial Shade with no full-sun entry. The record converted a twice-hedged tolerance into a listed recommended exposure, drawn from MOBOT's one-line "Sun: Full sun to part shade" header while ignoring the prose on the same page that walks it back.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Not one of the quotes says "moderate" or anything meaning it, and all four admissible sources say the opposite. NC State's structured field is literally "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage / Moist"; NC State prose says "a well-drained potting medium rich in organic matter"; MOBOT says "a peaty well-drained soil mix"; RHS says "moist but well-drained". The parenthetical gloss "(well-drained but moisture-holding)" is the researcher reconciling NC State's "Moist" checkbox with "Good Drainage" and then downgrading the result — a synthesis, not a source statement. The downgrade is in the harmful direction: Clemson's own factsheet for this plant warns "Root rot usually results from a soil mix that does not drain quickly or overly frequent watering."

water_dry_down_target — removed on audit: "through the pot" appears in no source. MOBOT's verbatim sentence is "Best to deeply water and then allow soils to nearly dry before applying an additional deep watering" — no depth is stated, and the same page rates the plant "Water: Medium", says "Water regularly but moderately during the growing season", and warns under Problems that "Leaves will drop if soils become too moist or too dry." The only admissible source that gives a depth at all is Clemson, which explicitly covers Dwarf Schefflera (S. arboricola) and says "let the soil dry to ½ inch deep before watering again." The record took the most aggressive available reading and then added a full-root-ball qualifier that no source supports, while relegating the direct conflict to a note about a different field (water_check_depth_cm).

water_regime — removed on audit: UGA W=3 reads "Soil mix can become moderately dry before re-watering." The record's own water_dry_down_target quotes that wording correctly, then the enum contradicts it: "moderately dry" is an explicitly hedged partial dry-down, while dry_thoroughly_between asserts a complete one. That W=3 is the driest of UGA's three bands is a rank inside a scheme whose driest option is still only "moderately" — a relative ordering is not an absolute claim about drying the rootball out. Nothing on any admissible page says thoroughly, completely, or bone dry for E. elegans; RHS's only watering sentence, "Water moderately when in growth," cuts the other way. The citation carrying this claim quotes just "Echeveria elegans | Mexican Snowball | 1-2 2 3 3 5" — no watering language at all. Care-critical, and the error direction is underwatering.

light_fc_min — removed on audit: UGA rates this species L=1-2. Band 1 ("Sunny light areas: At least 4 hours of direct sun") contains no foot-candle figure whatsoever, so for a plant that may sit in band 1 no fc floor is stated at all. The 200 comes only from band 2's "Over 200 ft-c, but not direct sun" — a threshold defining a generic light class shared by every plant coded 2 in the bulletin, not a measurement of E. elegans. The number appears nowhere in the citation quote that claims it (the row is bare codes); it exists only in the key citation, which itself declares "no value taken directly from this key." The record's own light_fc_good unknown says band 1 "is defined by hours of direct sun rather than foot-candles, so no preferred foot-candle figure is stated" — that reasoning kills the minimum too. Textbook class-level figure presented as a species value.

day_f_max — removed on audit: 75°F is lifted from UGA's T=2 class definition, "Average: 65°F night, 75°F day temperatures" — boilerplate attached identically to E. agavoides, Echinocereus reichenbachii and every other plant coded 2, not a figure UGA states about E. elegans. Compounding it, setting max equal to min makes 75 a hard ceiling, asserting that this species is documented to tolerate nothing above 75°F. UGA states no ceiling, no range and no tolerance for it; a succulent capped at 75°F day temperature is also a claim the source would not support. The row quote cited contains only the digit 2.

day_f_min — removed on audit: Same defect as day_f_max: 75 is the definition of UGA's generic "Average" temperature class, not a species measurement, and the citation's quote for this claim ("1-2 2 3 3 5") contains no temperature. The record disqualifies the H=3 numbers from the same table as class band rather than "a measured requirement for this species," and disqualifies the RHS H2 range as "a hardiness band, not a stated damage-onset temperature" — the T=2 numbers are band definitions by exactly those tests and should be null on the same grounds.

night_f_min — removed on audit: 65°F is the night half of UGA's T=2 class descriptor, a label definition applied to hundreds of species, not a night temperature UGA states for E. elegans. Taking the numbers out of a coding key while the record elsewhere refuses to take numbers out of that same key (humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max) is an unreconciled internal contradiction, and the citation quote backing it holds no temperature text.

night_f_max — removed on audit: Class-band derivation as with night_f_min, plus false precision: min=max=65 encodes a zero-width night range, implying a documented optimum of exactly 65°F with no tolerance either side. UGA gives one illustrative pair for a three-way Cool/Average/Warm split; it states no upper night limit for this species, and no admissible source does.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: No admissible source says fast or sharp drainage for E. elegans, and the record's own citations say something weaker. NC State's drainage field for this species reads "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Occasionally Dry"; RHS reads "Moisture Well–drained." Fast is a step beyond both and that conflict with the quoted NC State wording is never reconciled. The quote actually attached to the claim — "a peat-free, loam-based potting compost with added extra grit" — describes a mix composition, not a drainage rate, and loam-based is the heavier end of RHS's compost families; extra grit relative to that baseline does not establish the fast band.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The array entry "full sun with protection from hot sun" is a phrase no source states. I pulled the live RHS page (504241): the structured field reads "Position | Full sun" and, separately, the cultivation prose reads "Grow in cactus compost in full light with protection from hot sun." The record fused a value from one field with a modified fragment of another sentence — RHS says "full light with protection from hot sun", never "full sun with protection from hot sun". Worse, RHS's Position/Aspect/Exposure fields describe UK growing conditions for a plant RHS rates hardiness H2 ("tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5)") and whose suggested locations are "Houseplants | Patio and container plants | Sub-tropical | Conservatory and greenhouse" — i.e. a glasshouse position, not an outdoor sun exposure. Publishing it alongside "partial shade" also makes the field self-contradictory, and it contradicts the NC State species page the record itself cites: Cultural Conditions Light = "Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)" plus the explicit warning "Direct sunlight can scorch the leaves." fertilize_active_months — removed on audit: No quote in the record contains a month. Penn State (verified verbatim) says only "The growing season for zebra plants occurs in spring and summer"; RHS says only "When in growth ... once or twice." The months 3-8 come from a Northern-Hemisphere meteorological mapping of "spring and summer" that neither source states, and the plant is native to the South African Cape, where that mapping is inverted. The record applies an inconsistent standard: it explicitly refuses NC State's "2-6 hours" for direct_sun_hours_max because it is "the generic gloss on its Partial Shade category rather than a measurement for this species", then performs exactly that category-to-number derivation here.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: No source states a drainage rate. Where the sources do give a structured drainage value they give a middle band, not a fast one — NC State's Cultural Conditions read "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage | Occasionally Dry", and RHS's Growing Conditions read "Moisture: Well–drained." "fast" is the researcher's upgrade of "well-drained" to the top band, taken from text that never characterizes speed, and the record cites no structured field that supports it.

common_name — removed on audit: The citation label leads with "is_houseplant true; common_name Zebra Haworthia", but the attached quote never contains "Zebra Haworthia" — it says "The zebra plant is grown as an ornamental...", which supports "Zebra Plant" at most. water_regime — removed on audit: The value dry_thoroughly_between is the driest option in the WaterRegime enum (garden-gnome/app/models/models.py:115-125: keep_moist, keep_barely_moist, dry_surface_between, dry_thoroughly_between), and it is contradicted by both species-level sources while resting on a genus-level one. (1) GENUS-LEVEL SUPPORT ONLY: the sole quote that says 'dry out between waterings' is Clemson's Peperomia spp. factsheet, and I confirmed on the live page that the sentence sits under the genus watering section ('Peperomia prefers to dry out between waterings'), not under the Baby Rubber Plant entry. The species entry says only 'It has low water needs,' which states no dry-down endpoint. (2) SPECIES-LEVEL SOURCES SAY OTHERWISE: NC State's species page states verbatim 'It is intolerant of wet soil, very dry soil, or very drafty sites' — an explicit contraindication of drying thoroughly. Missouri Botanical Garden (I confirmed kempercode=b609 is Peperomia obtusifolia, 'baby rubber plant') states 'Water moderately but consistently, allowing the soils to almost dry on top before rewatering' and lists 'Water: Medium'. (3) A BETTER-MATCHED ENUM VALUE WAS PASSED OVER: dry_surface_between is a literal match for MOBOT's 'almost dry on top' and is compatible with NC State's 'prefers dry soil' plus 'intolerant of very dry soil'. The corpus already uses it for comparable plants (Rubber Plant, Dragon Tree, Peace Lily). (4) THE RECORD CONCEDES THE POINT TWICE: water_dry_down_target says 'but not to bone dry', and a separate citation says MOBOT 'gives a wetter dry-down than the extension sources'. A regime whose own dry-down note negates the word 'thoroughly' is not a supported value. (5) MIS-CITATION: the citation labelled '...; water_regime dry_thoroughly_between' offers the NC State quote as evidence for the value, but that quote is the sentence that rules it out. (6) HARM DIRECTION: this pushes chronic under-watering onto a species an admissible source explicitly calls intolerant of very dry soil. Either dry_surface_between or null is honest here; dry_thoroughly_between is not.

That is a dry-down regime, the opposite of keep_moist, and the record encodes BOTH (water_regime=keep_moist alongside a 2.5 cm dry-down target) without reconciling them. The two supporting quotes are weaker than they look: MoBot's 'evenly moist soil' sits in a Culture block whose own structured rating is 'Water: Medium' (verified on plantfinder.mobot.org) and whose 'Suggested Use: Annual, Water Plant' framing is outdoor/landscape, not the potted indoor culture this record describes; NC State's 'requires a moist potting mix' is a one-clause aside in a general description, and the Problems section on that same NC State page reads 'Overwatering can cause yellowing of the leaves and rotting of the stems.' Failure scenario: a keeper following keep_moist never lets the top inch dry, the mix stays saturated in a pot Clemson says must drain fully, and the plant develops the stem rot NC State names. The defensible value is a dry-down regime, not keep_moist.

light_fc_min — removed on audit: Refuted: the number 150 is not stated as a minimum for this species anywhere. Clemson's band definition, quoted in the record itself and verified verbatim, reads 'Medium (minimum 100 to 150 ft-c, 200 to 500 preferred)', and the table heading reads 'Medium light (100 to 150 ft-c)'. The record silently takes the top of a stated minimum RANGE and presents it as the floor. Worse, the species' own entry in that table is asterisked 'Dracaena sanderana*' with the footnote '*May also be conditioned to grow in low light' — and Clemson's Low band minimum is 100 ft-c, so the one piece of species-specific information on that page points downward, not to 150. light_fc_good=200 survives (it is the stated bottom of the preferred range); light_fc_min does not.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: Refuted as an unresolved source conflict presented as a settled two-value answer. MoBot's 'Sun: Part shade to full shade' is verbatim and real, but RHS — an admissible source the record already cites twice, for name_note and fertilize_interval_days — lists 'Position: Full sun, Partial shade' with 'Aspect: East-facing or South-facing or West-facing' and cultivation text 'Grow in peat-free, loam-based potting compost in full light with shade from hot sun.' The two admissible sources disagree at BOTH ends: RHS admits full sun (which the record excludes) and does not admit full shade (which the record asserts). The Clemson 'supporting' citation says only 'a shady area' for summering outdoors, which does not distinguish part shade from full shade and so cannot break the tie. The record had the contradicting RHS page in hand and did not surface the conflict.

night_f_min — removed on audit: Refuted as a repurposed management threshold. Clemson's 65 degrees F appears under the section heading 'Growing Lucky Bamboo Outdoors' as the rule for when to end outdoor summering ('It must be brought back indoors before nighttime temperatures drop below 65 degrees F'); it is not stated as a minimum night temperature for the plant in cultivation, and Clemson never says the plant is harmed below it. The record itself recognized this framing — its own unknowns entry says 'Clemson's 65 degrees F is a bring-indoors management threshold, not a damage-onset temperature' — and then used the same number as a physiological night floor anyway. Two other admissible sources put the floor lower and were not reconciled: RHS rates this plant H1B, defined on the same page as 'can be grown outside in the summer (10 - 15)' degrees C, i.e. roughly 50-59 F; UF/IFAS EP149 (which does name D. sanderiana in Table 1) says 'Plants should be kept in areas above 60 degrees F at all times.' Three admissible floors (65, 60, 50-59) exist and the record recorded one as fact. Error direction is conservative — a keeper warned at 64 F suffers false alarms, not a dead plant — but the value is not established by the quote as a night_f_min.
